When the sad spectacle at Clemson had ended Tuesday, with Dabo Swinney once again going into full lockdown mode to protect a track record that doesn't seem particularly relevant anymore, the keypad on the door to the press conference room no longer accepted his code. 
 "Well, maybe I won't be here," he quipped to reporters, lightening the room with gallows humor after he had been peppered with tough, but fair questions about the program's problems. "Some of y'all might get your wish." 
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Despite Swinney being wrong about one thing — the majority at Clemson wants him to evolve, not leave — the symbolism of his failed escape was hard to miss. 
 However the current standoff at Clemson gets resolved — will the school really fire the guy who delivered two national championships; will Dabo be willing to entertain a holistic program reset that removes some of his autonomy? — there must be clarity in the next couple weeks on whether he's exiting the building or entering a new phase of his career.
 In the midst of a nightmare Clemson season that has brought all the long-simmering issues around Swinney to the surface, a fault line has emerged: You cannot have a football coach who refuses to accept that major changes are necessary while the Clemson administration is building out a centralized front office for roster spending across all sports that would be overseen by athletic director Graham Neff, stripping the coach of some authority over personnel decisions. 
 But the gap between where Swinney sits (things are fine, just a rough patch, etc.) and what Clemson sees (this isn't working and a course correction is necessary) is an old tale that has ushered a number of legendary coaches into a retirement they weren't ready to accept.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement It also may be one of the last times it plays out like this in college sports. 
 "People wanna get mad because they only wanna look at two years, and that's fair game," Swinney told reporters. "But I've also coached 250 games, and that's fair game, too. I lost my first game and I lost my 250th game, but I'd take Game 2 through Game 249." 
 Clemson coach Dabo Swinney has gone 193-57 in 19 seasons with the Tigers.
 (AP Photo/Jacob Kupferman) What we're seeing with Swinney isn't merely about the end of an era at Clemson. It's about the entire concept of the God-tier, statue-worthy coach crumbling as the sport professionalizes.
 Though Swinney is still relatively young — he turns 57 on Friday — he is one of only four current coaches who will, by force of longevity and accomplishment, one day get a statue at their school. It's Swinney, Kirby Smart at Georgia, Kirk Ferentz at Iowa and Curt Cignetti at Indiana. Maybe Mario Cristobal at Miami gets there if he wins a couple national titles. 
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement But that's the list. There's really nobody else on the horizon trending toward that kind of résumé or likely to build the kind of sprawling legacy like Nick Saban, Bobby Bowden, Tom Osborne and Joe Paterno, where their image is forever intertwined with the place they coached.
 We can run through all the reasons it's a dying model. It's the money getting so big that few will remain hungry to sustain excellence over decades. It's the pressure of the job in the Internet era. It's the parity ushered in by NIL, making long-term dominance almost impossible. For some, it may even be the NFL offering a situation where you don't have to spend time courting donors and kissing babies. 
 Ultimately, though, the Swinney dynamic is about power. And when you won like Swinney, you got it almost unconditionally. If you wanted a raise for yourself and the staff, the athletic director and president practically offered a blank check. If you needed a facility built, donors opened up their pocketbooks. If a player got in trouble off the field, the coach had the final word while university officials swallowed the embarrassment. 
 Presidents may have technically had the power and final authority over athletics, but everyone knew that when push came to shove, nobody really had the power to say, "No." 
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Swinney has been one of the few remaining with that kind of juice. However this gets resolved, you'll never see it at Clemson — or perhaps anywhere else — again.
 Because what's happening in college sports right now is akin to the revolution in pro sports a decade or so ago when NFL and NBA franchises realized that having the same person be the coach and general manager was a recipe for disaster. 
 The jobs are too big. Contracts and salary caps are too complex. It is healthier in most cases for the person holding the players accountable not to be the same one responsible for negotiating their salary. 
 That fundamentally goes against the tradition of college sports, where recruits picked a school based on a variety of factors but none bigger than who would be coaching them. That's how the cult of the coach was built, how power was accumulated. Unlike the pros, where coaches are also highly paid but considered replaceable, the coach was central to everything happening in a college program.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement That distinction still exists, to a degree. It's why the coaching carousel is the biggest animating topic in college football almost from the first week of the season to the last. Coaching decisions are the foundation of whether a program will rise or fall. 
 But coaches are also now cogs in a much larger machine. Though the general manager/personnel department/athletic director/booster collective structure looks a little different everywhere, with head coaches having varying degrees of power when it comes to player selection and contract value, the front office has to be more collaborative by nature. 
 For someone like Swinney, it's a big change — and one he has not shown a willingness yet to accept. But he may not have much choice at this point. Fans are up in arms. Administrators are frustrated. His $57 million buyout looms as a leverage point, but college sports has changed. No one who is 13-10 over the last two seasons can credibly tell a fan base or the people responsible for funding an athletic budget that their power and authority over big decisions can't be questioned or even taken away. 
 It doesn't work like that anymore. If you're Swinney, other than a temporary bruise on his ego, why would you want the help? 
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement We have seen ugly endings to legendary careers before. Bowden was forced into retirement before he was ready to give it up. TCU had already built the statue for Gary Patterson before firing him in the middle of his 21st season. Last year, Mike Gundy was as defiant and petulant as you'd expect the greatest coach in Oklahoma State history to be after two decades, but it didn't stave off the end. 
 The more college sports starts to mimic the pros, those types of careers will either become impossible or exceedingly rare. Once the current generation of statue coaches goes extinct, we might not see them again, replaced by a more transactional relationship that will have its own set of pluses and minuses. 
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Swinney is one of the very few who won enough for long enough to enjoy the kind of power that a Bowden or Paterno had in their heyday. But the championships he thought would buy him enough goodwill and time to get through a couple bad seasons have instead led Swinney into a public relations debacle, with fans wanting evidence of a new strategy rather than a recitation of his accolades every time he gets asked why Clemson isn't winning anymore. 
 Swinney has a couple weeks to accept a new coaching reality or face the possibility of his employer resolving the situation with drastic action. And if there does come a point where he's locked out for real, it won't just be a coach walking out the door for the final time but the entire coaching model that the previous era of college sports once aspired to achieve.
